title: Plan the Restart, Not the Streak
hook: Missing once rarely ends a routine. Not knowing how to restart often does.
actions: Skip the urge to repay missed days
research_query: How do habit lapse recovery plans, self-compassion, and all-or-nothing thinking affect re-engagement with health behaviors?
visual: Pebble steps around a broken streak counter toward a restart button.
rationale: A forgiving alternative to streak pressure with clear, practical actions.
safety: Do not promise adherence or frame a lapse as a personal failure. Keep all actions optional.

title: The Mental Tab Handoff
hook: Why does the last task follow you into the next one?
actions: Leave the note where you will restart
research_query: What evidence links task interruption, resumption cues, external reminders, and attention residue?
visual: Pebble hands a glowing mental tab to a paper note.
rationale: A distinctive metaphor for an everyday attention problem with strong prop visuals.
safety: Avoid implying a diagnosis or claiming that the method removes intrusive thoughts.

title: Shrink the Choice Menu
hook: Too many good options can make starting harder.
actions: Cap the immediate menu at three
Hide choices you do not need now
research_query: What evidence links choice overload, defaults, cognitive load, and follow-through in everyday decisions?
visual: A giant menu folds down to three simple cards beside Pebble.
rationale: Turns decision friction into a concrete visual and a small environmental change.
safety: Do not claim choice is universally harmful. Preserve personal agency and accessible alternatives.

title: Make Notifications Ask Permission
hook: Your phone does not need a vote on every minute of your attention.
research_query: How do smartphone notifications, notification batching, and phone visibility affect attention and task performance?
visual: Notifications line up at a permission desk staffed by Pebble.
rationale: A practical attention boundary with unusually clear phone-based visuals.
safety: Keep exceptions for caregiving, work, safety, and accessibility needs.

title: Build the Bad-Day Version
hook: If your routine only works on good days, it may need a smaller version.
actions: Define the minimum version in advance
Return to the full version without repayment
research_query: What evidence links smaller behavior targets, contextual cues, and flexible goal adjustment with habit maintenance?
visual: A large routine card folds into a small bad-day card.
rationale: Supportive, realistic, and useful when time or energy changes.
safety: Avoid ableist assumptions, productivity pressure, and claims about treating low mood or fatigue.

title: Build a Tiny Start Button
hook: Make the first move so small it feels like pressing Play.
actions: Name only the first physical move
research_query: What evidence links implementation intentions, graded tasks, and reduced activation effort with task initiation?
visual: A comically small start button sits beside an oversized task.
rationale: A compact, visual way to reduce the pressure of getting started.
safety: Do not present task initiation trouble as proof of a condition or guarantee completion.

title: Create a Reset Station
hook: Your environment can offer a pause before you remember to ask for one.
research_query: How do environmental cues, object placement, and implementation intentions affect repeated everyday behaviors?
visual: Pebble deposits and retrieves everyday objects at a small reset station.
rationale: A simple environmental system with recurring set and prop potential.
safety: Offer cheap, small-space alternatives and avoid claiming that cues work for everyone.

title: Can a Messy Counter Feel Noisy?
hook: Why can six objects compete for your attention without making a sound?
actions: Corral loose items in one tray
Lower what sits in your direct sightline
Use a temporary basket instead of a full cleanup
research_query: What evidence connects visual clutter, selective attention, cognitive load, and perceived stress in adults?
visual: Counter objects make noise marks that fade as one small area clears.
rationale: A relatable hook and strong before-and-after visual without requiring a full cleanup.
safety: Treat clutter as optional visual load, not a moral failure. Evidence may be limited and must be reviewed carefully.

title: Your Best Posture Is the Next One
hook: Your body may prefer position changes over one supposedly perfect posture.
actions: Move before discomfort becomes the only cue
research_query: What evidence compares posture variation and dynamic sitting with maintaining one ergonomic posture during prolonged sitting?
visual: Pebble rotates through sitting, leaning, standing, and stretching.
rationale: A fresh correction to rigid posture advice with movement-rich visuals.
safety: No pain treatment or injury-prevention claims. Encourage professional advice for persistent pain or specific access needs.

title: The One-Study Headline Check
hook: A health headline can sound certain even when the research is not.
actions: Look for the number of participants
Check what the study actually measured
research_query: How do study design, sample size, replication, and headline framing affect the reliability of wellness claims?
visual: A bold headline shrinks beside a plain-language study card.
rationale: A practical media-literacy routine that strengthens the whole channel's evidence culture.
safety: Present these as screening questions, not a complete evidence appraisal or a reason to dismiss all single studies.
